title: Your Thinking Toolkit
objective: After this level you can run a new claim through the tree's key checks: the argument, the evidence, the cause, your own biases and the source.
summary: Dewey's disordered rooms show the toolkit at work: rival explanations, tests, then belief. The SEP's checklist and a check on your own bias complete it.

cards.headline: You come home. Your things are thrown everywhere. What happened?
cards.body: John Dewey used exactly this scene in How We Think, back in 1910. Remember him from Level 1? Follow what his man does next, and you'll see the thinking toolkit at work in one messy room.

cards.headline: Two stories, held open
cards.body: Dewey's man first thinks: burglary. Then a second explanation occurs to him. His children are mischievous, and they may have thrown things about. That rival explanation stops him from accepting the first idea dogmatically. Judgment is held in suspense.

cards.headline: Test, then believe
cards.body: If burglars did it, valuables would be missing. He checks a box: some things are gone, but he might have moved them himself, so that test isn't decisive. Then the silver in the sideboard, which the children wouldn't take: all gone. Windows and doors show signs of tampering. Only now does belief settle on burglary.

cards.headline: The checklist
cards.body: The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy suggests picturing critical thinking as a checklist, used in any order, selectively and more than once. Items include laying out possible solutions, deciding which evidence is relevant, judging the credibility of what others tell you, and accepting only what the evidence adequately supports. For a new claim: what's the argument, and its hidden premise? What's the evidence? What else could explain it? Who says so?

cards.headline: Check yourself too
cards.body: The last check points inward. People seek and interpret evidence in ways that favor what they already believe, often without noticing: confirmation bias. One remedy the encyclopedia names is holding off on a favorite explanation until the evidence rules out the others. That's just what Dewey's man did.

cards.headline: Toolkit: assembled
learned: Keep rival explanations open before you believe one
Test each idea by what it predicts you should find
Check the argument, evidence, alternatives and source
Check your own bias: hold off on favorite explanations

questions.prompt: In Dewey's example, what kept the man from simply concluding "burglary"?

options.label: A neighbor who had seen the burglars
options.rationale: No witness appears in the story.

options.label: A police report about the break-in
options.rationale: No report appears in the story.

options.label: A rival explanation: his mischievous children
His belief that burglaries never happen
options.rationale: He takes burglary seriously and tests it.

questions.explanation: Thinking of his mischievous children gave him a rival explanation, so he held judgment in suspense.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of Dewey's man in order, from first to last.
items: A second explanation occurs to him
Only now does belief settle on burglary
questions.explanation: Dewey's man first thinks burglary, then a second explanation occurs to him. He checks a box, which isn't decisive, then the silver in the sideboard. Only now does belief settle on burglary.

questions.prompt: The toolkit's first check takes a new claim's argument apart, looking for what the argument never says out loud: _____.

options.label: its signal words
options.rationale: Those are said; they are how you find the conclusion.

options.label: its explanation
options.rationale: An explanation is a different kind of reasoning, not a hidden part.

questions.explanation: An unstated premise is one an argument needs but never states, often the part most worth questioning.
